title: By ordinary law ministry must lead first; Romans 10 and Augustine
source_text: XVIII. Itaque, juxta legem ordinariam, ministerium illud necessarium est, ut aliquis doctrinae et Scripturae divinae cognitionem habeat, et fidem concipiat. Nec enim Spiritus sanctus in verbi Dei notitiam immediate nos ducit. Neque quod doctrinam caelestem amplectimur, et veneramur Scripturas, id facimus quopiam immediato Spiritus afflatu. Sed necesse est ut hac in re praeeuntes habeamus Ecclesiae ministros, et eos quibus nostra institutio commissa est, qui nobis doctrinam illam proponant et exponant, et Scripturam indicent, explicent et commendent. Et primum isto Ecclesiae testimonio movemur, ut de doctrina caelesti et Scriptura sacra bene sentiamus, et fidem ei habeamus, alias in perpetua ignoratione illius versaturi. Juxta illud Apostoli, Roman. 10. Quomodo credent ei de quo non audiverunt? Quomodo audient sine praedicante? Item, Fides est ex auditu: auditus per verbum Dei, id est, ex Dei mandato. Quo spectat illud Augustini toties decantatum, Non crederem Evangelio, nisi me Catholicae Ecclesiae commoveret authoritas. Loquitur enim in persona ejus qui ad fidem introducitur, et aliquam de Evangelii divina veritate persuasionem habere incipit. Nam Ecclesiae communis consensus et testimonium ordinarie est primum incitamentum, quo inducimur ad aliquam Scripturae fidem adhibendam. Atque etiam inter ipsos fideles, quum dubitatio oritur de aliquo libro et dogmate divino, fatemur constans atque uniforme Ecclesiae testimonium argumentum esse maximi ponderis et momenti, cui judicium proprium opponere hominis sit insolentis atque temerarii. Praesertim vero, quum agitur de libri alicujus sacri rejectione vel admissione, agnoscimus perpetuum Ecclesiae Judaicae et Christianae consensum argumentum esse ineluctabile, et cui quemvis cedere oporteat.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, according to the ordinary law, that ministry is necessary in order that someone have knowledge of divine teaching and Scripture, and conceive faith. For the Holy Spirit does not lead us immediately into knowledge of God's Word. Nor do we embrace heavenly teaching and revere the Scriptures by some immediate breathing of the Spirit. But it is necessary that in this matter we have going before us the Church's ministers, and those to whom our instruction has been committed, who propose and set forth that teaching to us, and point out, explain, and commend Scripture. And first by that Church testimony we are moved to think well of heavenly teaching and sacred Scripture, and to give it faith, otherwise we would remain in perpetual ignorance of it. According to that of the Apostle, Romans 10: How will they believe him of whom they have not heard? How will they hear without a preacher? Likewise, Faith is from hearing: hearing through the Word of God, that is, from God's command. To which looks that oft-sung saying of Augustine, I would not believe the Gospel unless the authority of the Catholic Church moved me. For he speaks in the person of one who is being introduced to faith, and begins to have some persuasion of the Gospel's divine truth. For the Church's common consensus and testimony is ordinarily the first incentive by which we are led to apply some faith to Scripture. And even among the faithful themselves, when doubt arises about some book and divine dogma, we confess that the Church's constant and uniform testimony is an argument of the greatest weight and moment, to which for a person to oppose his own judgment is insolent and rash. Especially when it concerns the rejection or admission of some sacred book, we acknowledge that the perpetual consensus of the Jewish and Christian Church is an ineluctable argument, and one to which anyone ought to yield.
pass_b_english: So under the ordinary law that ministry is necessary if someone is to know divine teaching and Scripture and conceive faith. The Holy Spirit does not lead us straight into knowledge of God's Word. Nor do we embrace heavenly teaching and revere the Scriptures by some immediate breath of the Spirit. In this matter we need the Church's ministers going before us, and those entrusted with our instruction, who propose and set out that teaching and who point out, explain, and commend Scripture.

First that Church testimony moves us to think well of heavenly teaching and sacred Scripture and to give it faith; otherwise we would stay forever ignorant of it. As the Apostle says (Romans 10): "How will they believe him of whom they have not heard? How will they hear without a preacher?" Likewise: "Faith comes from hearing; and hearing through the Word of God" — that is, from God's command. Here belongs Augustine's oft-sung line: "I would not believe the Gospel unless the Catholic Church's authority moved me." He speaks in the person of someone being brought into faith, who is beginning to have some persuasion of the Gospel's divine truth.

For the Church's common consensus and testimony is ordinarily the first incentive that leads us to give Scripture some faith. And even among the faithful themselves, when doubt arises about some book or divine dogma, we confess that the Church's constant, uniform testimony is an argument of the greatest weight and moment; for a person to set his own judgment against it is insolent and rash. Especially when the question is rejecting or admitting some sacred book, we acknowledge that the perpetual consensus of the Jewish and Christian Church is an inescapable argument, one to which anyone ought to yield.
